claims.text: Service exposure transforms metastable Mg-containing phases into stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
The newly formed Mg-rich intermetallic compounds preferentially form or grow along grain boundaries.
Intermetallic formation increases local chemical heterogeneity.
The increased heterogeneity and Mg-rich intermetallics intensify micro-galvanic coupling.
Intermetallic evolution disrupts the continuity and protective character of the oxide film.
The oxide-film disruption and micro-galvanic coupling increase corrosion rates relative to the as-cast state.
The oxide-film disruption increases high-temperature oxidation rates relative to the as-cast state.
The as-cast alloy has a non-equilibrium microstructure containing metastable Mg-rich phases.
The initial Mg-containing alloy contains solid-solution regions together with incipient intermetallic phases.
The initial state possesses a protective oxide layer.
Controlled aging or environmental exposure will measurably increase the volume fraction of stable Mg-rich intermetallics.
Aged or exposed specimens will have higher corrosion current densities than as-cast controls.
Aged or exposed specimens will exhibit greater high-temperature oxide mass gain or spallation than as-cast controls.
The as-cast baseline has a lower fraction of stable intermetallics than the aged or exposed state.
Holding composition fixed ensures similar initial microstructures across specimens.
The selected alloy composition maintains a density below 6 g/cm³.
The transformation kinetics and resulting corrosion or oxidation effects may vary with minor composition changes and processing history.
Failure to observe both increased stable Mg-rich intermetallics and corresponding corrosion, oxidation, or oxide-integrity degradation would falsify the hypothesis.
